### Filter to Unique Requests

```{r}
# duplicate requests store the id of the original "parent" request in 'service_request_parent_id' 
# is.na checks for distinct potholes requests that returns true if NA in 'service_request_parent_id' 
pothole_unique <- pothole |> 
  mutate(is_unique = is.na(service_request_parent_id))

# orignal vs duplicates 
pothole_unique |> 
  count(is_unique) |> 
  mutate(share = n/sum(n))
```

69% of pothole service requests are unique

```{r}
# monthly potholes (unique)
pothole_monthly <- pothole_unique |> 
  # data to month 
  mutate(month = yearmonth(date_requested)) |> 
  # complete months only
  filter(month >= yearmonth('2016 Jun'),
         month <= yearmonth('2026 Oct')) |>
  group_by(month) |> 
  summarise(
    requests_unique = sum(is_unique), # distinct requests
    total_reports = n(),              # all requests including duplicates
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) |> 
  as_tsibble(index = month)
pothole_monthly
```

```{r}
pothole_daily <- pothole_unique |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(date_requested)) |>
  count(day, name = "requests") |>
  as_tsibble(index = day)

# any days missing
has_gaps(pothole_daily)

# gaps
pothole_daily |>
  count_gaps() |>
  arrange(desc(.n))
```

### Investigating the Lead Times

```{r}
lead_time <- pothole_unique |>
  select(date_requested, date_closed) |>
  mutate(
    date_requested = as.Date(date_requested),
    date_closed = as.Date(date_closed),
    month = floor_date(date_requested, unit = "month"),
    lead_time = as.numeric(date_closed - date_requested)
  )

mo_lead_time <- lead_time |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(
    avg_lead_time = mean(lead_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_closed = sum(!is.na(lead_time)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

scale_factor <- max(mo_lead_time$avg_lead_time, na.rm = TRUE) /
  max(pothole_monthly$requests_unique, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = mo_lead_time,
            aes(x = month, y = avg_lead_time, color = "Lead Time")) +
  geom_line(data = pothole_monthly |> mutate(month = as.Date(month)),
            aes(x = month, y = requests_unique * scale_factor, 
                color = "Requests")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Average Lead Time (Days)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . / scale_factor,
      name = "Monthly Requests")) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Lead Time" = "#0072B2",
      "Requests" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Pothole Request Lead Time Per Month",
    x = "Month") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.y.left = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.text.y.left = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "#D55E00"),
    axis.text.y.right = element_text(color = "#D55E00")
  )

ggplot(pothole_monthly, aes(x = month, y = requests_unique)) +
  geom_line()
```

### Weekly lead time

```{r}
lead_time_weekly <- lead_time |>
  filter(is.na(lead_time) | lead_time >= 0) |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date_requested, unit = "week")) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(
    avg_lead_time_w = mean(lead_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_requests_w    = n(),
    n_closed_w      = sum(!is.na(lead_time)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(week > as.Date("2016-05-15"))

# Limits from the full period, so every snapshot shares the same scales
lead_max     <- max(lead_time_weekly$avg_lead_time_w, na.rm = TRUE)
req_max      <- max(lead_time_weekly$n_requests_w, na.rm = TRUE)
scale_factor <- lead_max / req_max

ggplot(lead_time_weekly) +
  geom_line(aes(x = week, y = n_requests_w * scale_factor, color = "Requests")) +
  geom_line(aes(x = week, y = avg_lead_time_w, color = "Lead Time")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Average Lead Time (Days)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / scale_factor, name = "Number of Weekly Requests")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Lead Time" = "#0072B2", "Requests" = "black")) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = as.Date(c("2016-05-15", "2026-10-31")),
    ylim = c(0, lead_max)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Pothole Request Lead Time Per Week",
    x = "Week"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.y.left  = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.text.y.left   = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "black"),
    axis.text.y.right  = element_text(color = "black")
  )
```

#### 4-week rolling-average

```{r}

lead_time_weekly <- lead_time |>
  filter(is.na(lead_time) | lead_time >= 0) |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date_requested, unit = "week")) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(
    avg_lead_time_w = mean(lead_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum_lead_w      = sum(lead_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_requests_w    = n(),
    n_closed_w      = sum(!is.na(lead_time)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(week > as.Date("2016-05-15")) |>
  arrange(week) |>
  mutate(
    # 4-week rolling average, weighted by closed requests, roughly centered
    roll_lead_w = slide_dbl(sum_lead_w, sum, .before = 2, .after = 1, .complete = TRUE) /
      slide_dbl(n_closed_w, sum, .before = 2, .after = 1, .complete = TRUE)
  )

# # 8-week rolling average, weighted by closed requests, roughly centered
# mutate(
#   roll_lead_w = slide_dbl(sum_lead_w, sum, .before = 4, .after = 3, .complete = TRUE) /
#     slide_dbl(n_closed_w, sum, .before = 4, .after = 3, .complete = TRUE)
# )

# Limits from the full period, so every snapshot shares the same scales
lead_max     <- max(lead_time_weekly$avg_lead_time_w, na.rm = TRUE)
req_max      <- max(lead_time_weekly$n_requests_w, na.rm = TRUE)
scale_factor <- lead_max / req_max
last_complete <- lead_time_weekly |>
  filter(n_closed_w / n_requests_w >= 0.95) |>
  pull(week) |>
  max()
```

```{r}
ggplot(lead_time_weekly) +
  geom_line(aes(x = week, y = n_requests_w * scale_factor, color = "Requests"))  +
  geom_line(aes(x = week, y = roll_lead_w, color = "Lead Time"),
            linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Average Lead Time (Days)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / scale_factor, name = "Number of Weekly Requests")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Lead Time" = "#0072B2", "Requests" = "black")) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = as.Date(c("2016-05-15", "2021-10-31")),
    ylim = c(0, lead_max)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Pothole Request Lead Time Per Week (2016-2022)",
    subtitle = "4-week rolling average",
    x = "Week"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.y.left  = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.text.y.left   = element_text(color = "#0072B2"),
    axis.title.y.right = element_text(color = "black"),
    axis.text.y.right  = element_text(color = "black")
  )-> p_lead_time_5year_16_22

ggsave('figures/average_lead_time_weekly(2025-2022).png', plot = p_lead_time_5year_16_22, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

## EDA

```{r}
daily_requests <- pothole_monthly |> 
  mutate(
    days = lubridate::days_in_month(as.Date(month)),
    unique_per_day = requests_unique / days,
    reports_per_day = total_reports / days
  )
```

```{r}
daily_requests |> autoplot(reports_per_day) +
  labs(
    title = 'Total Pothole Requests per Day',
    y = 'Number of total reports'
  )
```

Average requests per day for each month.

```{r}
daily_requests |> autoplot(unique_per_day) +
  labs(
    title = 'Unique Pothole Requests per Day',
    y = 'Number of unique requests'
  )
```

Average unique requests per day for each month.

```{r}
pothole_monthly |>
  mutate(dup_share = 1 - requests_unique / total_reports) |>
  autoplot(dup_share) +
  labs(title = 'Share of Pothole Reports That Are Duplicates',
       y = 'Duplicate share', x = NULL)
```

Both the total and unique requests show recurring seasonal fluctuations, with pronounced peaks in 2017, 2019, and 2023. Unique requests show a similar pattern, but with smaller peaks, suggesting that duplicate reports increase overall reporting activity. Overall, the recurring peaks suggest a seasonal pattern in pothole reports, while unique requests provide a clearer measure of distinct reported incidents.

```{r}
train_data |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(month),
    month_year = year(date) + if_else(month(date) >= 10, 1, 0),
    w_month = factor(month.abb[month(date)],
                     levels = month.abb[c(10:12, 1:9)])
  ) |> 
  filter(month_year >= 2017, month_year <= 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = w_month, y = requests_unique,
             colour = factor(month_year), group = month_year)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal plot by rainy season: unique pothole requests",
    y = "Unique pothole requests per month", colour = "month_year",
    x = 'Month'
  ) -> p_seasonal_plot

ggsave('figures/seasonal_plot.png', plot = p_seasonal_plot,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_seasonal_plot
```

The seasonal plot shows a recurring pattern in unique pothole requests during rainy seasons. Requests generally rise in the winter months, especially from January to March, then decline toward summer. However, the timing and size of each year’s peak vary, suggesting that winter patterns are less stable than seasonal patterns in summer and early fall, when the number of requests remains consistent.

### Decomposition

```{r}
train_data |> 
  model(classical_decomposition(requests_unique, type = 'additive')) |> 
  components() |> 
  autoplot() +
  labs(
    title = 'Additive decomposition (training)'
  )-> p_add_decomp

ggsave('figures/additive_decomposition_(training).png', plot = p_add_decomp,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_add_decomp
```

#### **Additive decomposition interpretation**

The remainder in the additive decomposition shows that errors stay close to 0 in summer, while rising from 1100 to 1200 in winter. This means errors are extremely large during winter and almost nonexistent in summer. For instance, a positive peak of 1000 means there were 1000 more requests than expected based on the trend and season, while negative dips indicate fewer pothole requests. Overall, this suggests winters are harder to predict than summers.

```{r}
train_data |> 
  model(classical_decomposition(requests_unique, type = 'multiplicative')) |> 
  components() |> 
  autoplot() +
  labs(
    title = 'Multiplicative decomposition (training)'
  )-> p_mult_decomp

ggsave('figures/multiplicative_decomposition_(training).png', plot = p_mult_decomp,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_mult_decomp
```

#### **Multiplicative decomposition interpretation**

The remainder in the multiplicative decomposition is distributed more evenly across the summer and winter months than in the additive decomposition. In multiplicative decomposition, if the remainder is close to 1, actual requests match the expected value. Peaks of about 1.5 indicate 50% more requests than expected, and negative dips of 0.8 indicate that actual requests were about 20% lower than expected. The multiplicative decomposition seems to fit monthly pothole requests slightly better because seasonal fluctuations are more similar in size across summer and winter months, indicating that variations are proportional to the level. This finding suggests that an ETS model with multiplicative components may fit the data better and produce more accurate forecasts.

```{r}
train_data |>
  model(STL(requests_unique ~ season(window = 'periodic'))) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = 'STL decomposition: original series (training period)') -> p_stl_decomp

ggsave('figures/STL_decomposition_(training).png', plot = p_stl_decomp, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_stl_decomp
```

The STL decomposition shows a strong, consistent annual pattern in unique service requests, with sharp increases occurring around the same time each year. The trend component fluctuates over time, rising around 2022, while the seasonal component remains fairly stable. The decomposition explains much of the variation in requests, but several large residual spikes indicate that unusual fluctuations remain unexplained. Overall, these findings support including annual seasonality in forecasting models while accounting for the rising trend.

```{r}
# log transformed decomposition
train_data |>
  model(STL(log(requests_unique) ~ season(window = 'periodic'))) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = 'STL decomposition: log series (training period)')
```

#### Outliers

```{r}
outliers_decomp <- train_data |> 
  model(STL(requests_unique ~ season(period=1), robust=TRUE)) |> 
  components()

# unusual observations
outliers_decomp |> 
  filter(
    remainder < quantile(remainder, 0.25) - 3 * IQR(remainder) |
      remainder > quantile(remainder, 0.75) + 3 * IQR(remainder)
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
outliers_decomp |> autoplot() +
  labs(
    title = 'Outliers - Unusual observations shown in STL remainder'
  )-> p_outliers

ggsave('figures/outliers.png', plot = p_outliers,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
p_outliers
```

The STL decomposition identified three unusually high observations in January 2017, January 2019, and January 2023, with approximately 2,996, 2,703, and 3,155 unique pothole requests, respectively. These observations were retained because they occurred during the high-rainfall season, likely reflecting genuine fluctuations in pothole reporting rather than data errors. While these observations do not establish causality, they highlight a potential limitation of relying solely on historical requests and suggest that incorporating external predictors, such as weather data, could help explain changes in request volume.

```{r}
train_data |>
  features(requests_unique, feat_stl) |>
  select(trend_strength, seasonal_strength_year) |>
  mutate(series = 'original', .before = 1) |>
  bind_rows(
    train_data |>
      features(log(requests_unique), feat_stl) |>
      select(trend_strength, seasonal_strength_year) |>
      mutate(series = 'log', .before = 1)
  )
```

```{r}
# Lag plots: each panel plots this month's value against the value
# k months earlier (lags 1 to 12). Points close to the diagonal line
# mean months that far apart tend to have similar values.
train_data |>
  gg_lag(requests_unique, geom = "point", lags = 1:12) +
  labs(title = "Lag plots: unique pothole requests (training period)",
       x = "Value k months earlier", y = "Current value")

```

```{r}
# the correlation between the series and its own past values, for lags up three years
# bars outside the dashed blue lines are larger than you'd expect from pure noise
train_data |>
  ACF(requests_unique, lag_max = 36) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "Autocorrelation: unique pothole requests (training period)")
```

### **Precipitation San Diego**

```{r}
precipitation_airport <- read_csv('Data/data.csv', skip = 1) 
```

```{r}
precipitation_airport <- precipitation_airport |> 
  rename(
    TAVG = `TAVG (Degrees Fahrenheit)`,
    TMAX = `TMAX (Degrees Fahrenheit)`,
    TMIN = `TMIN (Degrees Fahrenheit)`,
    PRCP = `PRCP (Inches)`
  )

# filter dates

prc <- precipitation_airport |> 
  as_tsibble(index = Date) |>  filter_index('2016-01-01' ~ .)

has_gaps(prc)
```

```{r}
prc |> autoplot(PRCP) +
  labs(
    title = 'Daily Precipitaion San Diego'
  )
```

```{r}
# monthly data
monthly_prcp <- prc |> 
  # index_by groups by time
  index_by(Month = yearmonth(Date)) |> 
  summarise(
    #na.rm = TRUE ingores missing values
    PRCP = sum(PRCP, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
monthly_prcp |> autoplot(PRCP) +
  labs(
    title = 'Monthly Precipitaion San Diego (International Airport Station)'
  )
```

```{r}
# monthly rainfall and pothole series joined and add last month's rainfall lag is created BEFORE splitting, so the first validation month (Nov 2025) gets October 2025's rainfall instead of NA.
model_data <- pothole_monthly |>
  left_join(
    monthly_prcp |> as_tibble() |> rename(month = Month),
    by = 'month'
  ) |>
  mutate(prcp_lag1 = lag(PRCP)) |>        
  filter_index('2016 Jun' ~ '2026 Oct')   

# Check: no missing rainfall values in the modeling period
model_data |> as_tibble() |> summarise(missing_prcp = sum(is.na(PRCP)),
                                       missing_lag  = sum(is.na(prcp_lag1)))
```

### TSLM Modeling

```{r}
# Time Series Linear Model - requests_unique

# Baseline TSLM Models
req_tslm <- train_data %>%
  model(
    auto_tslm = TSLM(requests_unique),
    tr_tslm = TSLM(requests_unique ~ trend()),
    sea_tslm = TSLM(requests_unique ~ season()),
    tslm = TSLM(requests_unique ~ trend() + season()),
    mean = MEAN(requests_unique),
    naive = NAIVE(requests_unique),
    snaive = SNAIVE(requests_unique),
    auto_tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP),
    tr_tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP + trend()),
    sea_tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP + season()),
    tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP + trend() + season())
  )

# assessing the model fits
glance(req_tslm) |>
  filter(.model %in% c("auto_tslm", "tr_tslm", "sea_tslm", "auto_tslm_p", "tr_tslm_p","tr_tslm_p", "sea_tslm_p", "tslm_p")) |>
  select(.model, r_squared, adj_r_squared, AIC, AICc, BIC) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(r_squared, adj_r_squared), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    across(c(AIC, AICc, BIC), ~ round(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Model",
      "R-squared",
      "Adjusted R-squared",
      "AIC",
      "AICc",
      "BIC"
    ),
    caption = "TSLM Model Comparison (ranked by AIC)"
  )

# assessing model accuracy
req_tslm |>
  accuracy() |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)

train_data %>%
  autoplot(requests_unique) +
  autolayer(
    fitted(req_tslm |> select("tslm")),
    .fitted,
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "TSLM: Monthly Pothole Requests",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Requests"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

These models served as a baseline, and the TSLM model including precipitation, trend and seasonality outperformed all of the other models. However, the model selection statistics were not optimal (R-squared = 0.68). Therefore, it could be advantageous to create more complex models that can capture the data more accurately. An important observation is that including the precipitation data in the model leads to improvements in the accuracy measurements. Therefore, precipitation will be included in the subsequent TSLM models.

```{r}
# Adding transformations and Fourier Terms

# find lambda for a Box-Cox transformation of the training data
lambda <- train_data |>
  features(requests_unique, features = guerrero) |>
  pull(lambda_guerrero)

# plot the transformed data side-by-side with the original data
p1 <- train_data |> autoplot(requests_unique) +
  labs(title = "Original Data", y = "Requests")

p2 <- train_data |> autoplot(log(requests_unique)) +
  labs(title = "Log Transformation", y = "Log requests")

p3 <- train_data |> autoplot(box_cox(requests_unique, -0.9)) +
  labs(title = "Box-Cox Transformation", y = "Box-Cox requests")

p1 / p2 / p3

req_transform <- train_data |>
  model(
    originalt = TSLM(requests_unique ~ trend() + season()),
    logt = TSLM(log(requests_unique) ~ trend() + season()),
    boxcoxt = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, -0.9) ~ trend() + season())
  )

req_transform |>
  select(originalt) |>
  gg_tsresiduals() &
  labs(title = "Residual Assessment - Original Data")

req_transform |>
  select(logt) |>
  gg_tsresiduals() &
  labs(title = "Residual Assessment - Log Transformation")

req_transform |>
  select(boxcoxt) |>
  gg_tsresiduals() &
  labs(title = "Residual Assessment - Box-Cox Transformation")

```

A visual inspection of the transformed data and residual plots suggested a slight preference for the Box-Cox Transformation over the Logarithmic Transformation.

```{r}
# New TSLM models with Box-Cox Transformation and Fourier Terms

# fit TSLM models with different seasonal specifications
tslm_models <- train_data %>%
  model(
    tslm = TSLM(requests_unique ~ trend() + season()),
    tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP + trend() + season()),
    bc_sea = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                    PRCP + trend() + season()),
    bc_f1 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 1)),
    bc_f2 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 2)),
    bc_f3 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 3)),
    bc_f4 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 4)),
    bc_f5 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 5))
  )

# assessing the model fits
glance(tslm_models) |>
  select(.model, r_squared, adj_r_squared, AIC, AICc, BIC) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(r_squared, adj_r_squared), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    across(c(AIC, AICc, BIC), ~ round(.x, 0))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Model",
      "R-squared",
      "Adjusted R-squared",
      "AIC",
      "AICc",
      "BIC"
    ),
    caption = "TSLM Model Comparison (ranked by AIC)"
  )

tslm_models |>
  accuracy() |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 0)

# plot the fitted values against the original training data
tslm_fits <- tslm_models |>
  augment()

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = train_data |> as_tibble(),
    aes(x = month, y = requests_unique),
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = tslm_fits |> as_tibble(),
    aes(x = month, y = .fitted, colour = .model),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs Fitted TSLM Models",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Unique Requests",
    colour = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Visually, the models appear to perform similarly. However, the model selection and accuracy statistics help to tease apart the details. The R-squared (0.716) and AIC values (-1699) show that the highest-ranking Box-Cox transformed model with k = 2 Fourier terms would be the better selection than the lowest-ranking baseline TSLM models (R-squared = 0.685 and 0.546, AIC = 1319 and 1358). However, the accuracy measurements tell a different story. The accuracy rankings show that the baseline TSLM models outperform all other models (RMSE = 300 and 360) and the Box-Cox transformed model with k = 2 Fourier terms exhibits the worst accuracy (RMSE = 475).

```{r}
# set up cross-validation method

# Set the final eligible CV origin
cv_cutoff <- max(train_data$month) - 12

# Keep only windows with 12 months of validation data available

  stretch_tsibble(.init = 60, .step = 12) |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  filter(max(month) <= cv_cutoff) |>
  ungroup()

cv_tslm_models <- cv_tslm |>
  model(
    tslm = TSLM(requests_unique ~ trend() + season()),
    tslm_p = TSLM(requests_unique ~ PRCP + trend() + season()),
    bc_sea = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                    PRCP + trend() + season()),
    bc_f1 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 1)),
    bc_f2 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 2)),
    bc_f3 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 3)),
    bc_f4 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 4)),
    bc_f5 = TSLM(box_cox(requests_unique, lambda) ~ 
                   PRCP + trend() +
                   fourier(period = 12, K = 5))
  )

# cv_fc <- cv_tslm_models |>
#   forecast(h = 12)

# future PRCP data for each cv window
cv_new_data <- cv_tslm |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  summarize(last_month = max(month), .groups = "drop") |>
  cross_join(
    train_data |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(month, PRCP)
  ) |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  filter(
    month > last_month,
    month <= last_month + 12
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  as_tsibble(key = .id, index = month)

# Check future precipitation data
cv_new_data |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  summarise(
    first_month = min(month),
    last_month = max(month),
    n = n(),
    missing_prcp = sum(is.na(PRCP)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# generate 12-month forecasts with future PRCP
cv_fc <- cv_tslm_models |>
  forecast(new_data = cv_new_data)

# cv_new_data |>
#   group_by(.id) |>
#   summarise(
#     n = n(),
#     missing_prcp = sum(is.na(PRCP)),
#     .groups = "drop"
#   )

# check forecast output
cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    missing = sum(is.na(.mean)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#glance(cv_tslm_models)

# cv_median <- cv_tslm_models |>
#   forecast(h = 12) |>
#   mutate(.median = quantile(requests_unique, 0.5)) |>
#   as_tibble()

# names(as_tibble(cv_fc))
# 
# head(as_tibble(cv_fc))

# Extract median forecasts
cv_median <- cv_fc |>
  mutate(
    .median = median(requests_unique)
  ) |>
  as_tibble()

# Extract mean forecasts
cv_forecasts <- cv_median |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(.model, .id, month, .median)

# Prepare actual validation observations
cv_actuals <- cv_new_data |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(.id, month) |>
  left_join(
    train_data |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(month, requests_unique),
    by = "month"
  )

# Calculate accuracy for each model and CV window
cv_accuracy <- cv_median |>
  select(.model, .id, month, .median) |>
  left_join(
    cv_actuals,
    by = c(".id", "month")
  ) |>
  group_by(.model, .id) |>
  summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((requests_unique - .median)^2)),
    MAE = mean(abs(requests_unique - .median)),
    MAPE = if (any(requests_unique == 0)) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      mean(abs((requests_unique - .median) /
                 requests_unique)) * 100
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

cv_accuracy_summary <- cv_accuracy |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(
    mean_RMSE = mean(RMSE),
    mean_MAE = mean(MAE),
    mean_MAPE = mean(MAPE, na.rm = TRUE),

  ) |>
  arrange(mean_RMSE)

knitr::kable(
  cv_accuracy_summary,

  caption = "Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation Accuracy"
)
```

The cross-validation reinforced that the basic TSLM models, with and without precipitation data, exhibited the best accuracy.

### **Exponential Smoothing Modeling**

```{r}
fit_ets <- train_data |> 
  model(
    # baseline
    ses = ETS(requests_unique ~ error('A') + trend('N') + season('N')),
    # additive errors and season
    hw_add = ETS(requests_unique ~ error('A') + trend('N') + season('A')),
    # multiplicative errors and season (winter adds error percentage)
    ets_mnm = ETS(requests_unique ~ error('M') + trend('N') + season('M')),
    # additive linear trend
    ets_mam = ETS(requests_unique ~ error('M') + trend('A') + season('M')),
    # adding a damped trend
    ets_madm = ETS(requests_unique ~ error('M') + trend('Ad') + season('M')),
    # auto selected
    ets_auto = ETS(requests_unique)
  )
```

#### **ETS(A,N,A) Interpretation**

The ETS(A,N,A) model uses additive errors and additive seasonality, with no trend. This model captures the seasonal patterns in the training data fairly well. However, it tends to underestimate unusually large spikes in requests.

The smoothing parameters are alpha and gamma. The alpha value (0.366) indicates that the model considers past observations while allowing the level to adjust as new data becomes available. The small gamma value (0.0001) indicates that the model expects the seasonal pattern to change very little and relies on a stable seasonal structure. The model’s AICc is 1678.17, and its RMSE is 424.24.

The model’s report indicates that January is expected to have about 700 more requests above the level, while the summer months are expected to have about 300 fewer requests below. Because of the additive components, these estimates remain the same every year regardless of the level.

```{r}
p_ets_mnm_fc
```

#### **ETS(M,N,M) Interpretation**

The ETS(M,N,M) model has multiplicative errors and seasonality and has no trend component. The fitted values closely match historical observations, capturing seasonal peaks and shifts in request volume.

The estimated smoothing parameters provide additional insight into the model’s performance. The alpha value (0.709) indicates that the model places more weight on recent observations, allowing it to adjust more quickly to changes in request volume. Similar to the ETS(A,N,A) model, the small gamma value (0.0001) assumes a stable seasonal pattern. The model’s AICc is 1585.37, and its RMSE is 502.06.

The model’s seasonal indices indicate that requests increase in January, February, March, and April, with estimated increases of about 74% above the level in March, 61% in February and January, and 39% in April, aligning with San Diego’s rainy season.

Confidence intervals are narrower during low-demand months and wider during peak months because the model’s multiplicative errors scale with the level. In contrast, ETS(A,N,A) confidence intervals remain the same in summer and winter.

## ARIMA Modeling

```{r}
data <- read.csv("Data/get_it_done_pothole_requests_datasd.csv")
head(data)

# Filter out duplicates (requests with parent ID's) and add month year column
data <- data |> 
  filter(is.na(service_request_parent_id)) |> 
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(date_requested))

# Check number of unique requests
nrow(data) # went down from 180k to 125k

# Aggregate into monthly intervals
data <- data |>
  count(Month, name = "Requests") |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month)

# check to make sure there are no months missing
has_gaps(data)

# Trim off first and last incomplete months
data <-  data |> filter_index('Jun 2016' ~ 'Oct 2026')
```

```{r}
# Train and validation
train <- data |> filter_index(. ~ 'Oct 2024')
validation <- data |> filter_index('Nov 2024' ~ 'Oct 2025')
test <- data |> filter_index('Nov 2025' ~ 'Oct 2026')

# plot to observe trend or seasonality
train |>
  autoplot() +
  scale_x_yearmonth(
    date_breaks = "6 months"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
train |> gg_season(Requests)
```

```{r}
# get differencing results
train |>
  features(Requests, unitroot_nsdiffs) |>
  bind_cols(
    train |> features(Requests, unitroot_ndiffs),
    train |> features(Requests, unitroot_kpss),
    train |> features(Requests, feat_stl)
  )
# pvalue is 0.1 meaning it is stationary (null hypothesis confirmed)
# Seasonal strength is < 0.64
# Seasonal and first order differencing not needed


# output the acf and pacf
train |> 
  ACF(Requests, lag_max = 48) |> 
  autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF, No Differencing, No Transformation")
# first two lags are significant, lag at 12 significant, MA(2)
# Shows spikes every 6 months

train |> 
  mutate(D12 = difference(Requests, lag = 12)) |>
  ACF(D12, lag_max = 36) |> 
  autoplot() + labs(title = "ACF, Seasonal Differencing, No Transformation")
# Shows spike at lag 12 but no patterns after that.
# Will validation with seasonal differencing and without.

train |> 
  PACF(Requests, lag_max = 36) |> 
  autoplot() + labs(title = "PACF, No Differencing, No Transformation")
# suggests AR(1) since 1st lag is significant, no seasonal AR components
# ACF suggest ARIMA (0,0,2)(0,0,1)[12] and PACF suggests ARIMA(1,0,0)
```

Candidate ARIMA models: 1) The ACF shows annual oscillations, with the highest auto-correlations at lags 1 and 2. Approximately every twelve months auto-correlations peak with similar strengths. This suggests a nonseasonal MA(2) component and a seasonal MA(1) component, since the next peaks do not occur at exactly at 24 or 36. 2) The PACF shows no seasonal patterns with a peak at the first lag and a majority of other lags with relatively weak auto-correlations. This plot indicates that a non-seasonal AR(1) component should be investigated with no seasonal components. 3) After seasonal differencing, the annual oscillations in the ACF plot went away and still shows a peak at 12, and peaks at the first two lags, meaning we can investigate the MA(2) component alongside seasonal differencing and a seasonal MA(1) term. 4) An automatically selected ARIMA model will also be fit and compared.

```{r}
# Fit all candidate arima models
arima_models <- train |> 
  model( arima100 = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(1,0,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)), # from pacf
         arima002 = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(0,0,2) + PDQ(0,0,1, period=12)), # from first acf,
         seasonal002 = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(0,0,2) + PDQ(0,1,1, period=12)), # from 2nd acf
         autoarima = ARIMA(Requests)
  )

# Output shows error with seasonal arima002 so will make slight adjustment
arima_models <- train |> 
  model( arima100 = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(1,0,0) + PDQ(0,0,0)), 
         sarima002 = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(0,0,2) + PDQ(0,0,1, period=12)), 
         sarima002_sd = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(0,0,2) + PDQ(0,1,0, period=12)), # simpler model
         autoarima = ARIMA(Requests, stepwise = FALSE, approx = FALSE) # optimize auto-selection
  )

# AICc
report(arima_models) |> 
  select(.model, AICc) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# Accuracy
accuracy(arima_models) |> 
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# Auto Arima Selection
auto_model <- arima_models |> select(autoarima)
report(auto_model)
```

Training Results: The auto-arima selected two non-seasonal and two seasonal AR coefficients, and chose a seasonal difference. This model has the lowest AICc of the four models, suggesting that it has the best balance between the model fit and complexity. It also has the lowest RMSE meaning that it has the lowest magnitude of errors for training data. The two best models based on the AICc and training RMSE are the auto-selected model and the ARIMA(0,0,2) with seasonal differencing.

```{r}
# Final Candidates
arima_models <- arima_models |>
  select(autoarima, sarima002_sd)

 # Residual ACF
arima_models |>
  augment() |>
  ACF(.innov) |>
  autoplot()

# LJung-Box Residual Auto-correlations significance
arima_models |>
  select(sarima002_sd) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 2) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# Residual Plots
arima_models |> 
  select(sarima002_sd) |> 
  gg_tsresiduals()

```

The Arima002010 residual ACF has a negative spike at 12, meaning it may not have captured the recurring seasonal patterns and may indicate that the residuals are not distributed with white noise. After testing this with the Ljung-Box test, the p-value is 0.1, larger than the 0.05 significance level cut-off. Therefore, we can move forward with evaluating these two models. These candidates will be evaluated against the validation set to test performance against unseen data.

```{r}
# Evaluate on Validation set
val_fc <- arima_models |> 
  forecast(new_data = validation)

accuracy(val_fc, validation) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)  |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# Plot Validation Forecast
val_fc |> 
  autoplot(validation) +
  facet_wrap(vars(.model), scales = "free_y")


```

Validation Results: Based on the RMSE, the Arima002 with seasonal differencing has produced the best forecast against the validation set, as it reduced the magnitude of errors best. However, the residual ACF plot suggests that the model may not have fully captured seasonal patterns. This trade-off must be taken into account. Next, transformations will be applied to test whether these can improve predictive performance.

```{r}
# Transform and re-select models if needed
train |> 
  features(Requests, guerrero)

# Use box-cox transformation with lambda = -0.9
train_transform <- train |>
  mutate(bc = box_cox(Requests, -0.9))

train_transform |>
  features(bc, unitroot_nsdiffs) |>
  bind_cols(
    train_bc |> features(bc, unitroot_ndiffs),
    train_bc |> features(bc, unitroot_kpss)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# ACF and PACF with differencing and boxcox
train_transform |> 
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(difference(bc, 12)), plot_type = 'partial', lag_max = 48)
# BoxCox candidates: ARIMA(0,1,2)(0,1,1), ARIMA(2,1,0)(2,1,0), and auto

# Log transform:
train_transform <- train_bc |>
  mutate(log = log(Requests))
train_log |>
  features(log, unitroot_nsdiffs) |>
  bind_cols(
    train_log |> features(log, unitroot_ndiffs),
    train_log |> features(log, unitroot_kpss)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# PACF and ACF with log transform and seasonal diff
train_transform |> 
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(log, 12), plot_type = 'partial', lag_max = 48)

# Log candidates: ARIMA(1,0,0)(1,1,0), ARIMA(0,0,4)(0,1,1), auto
```

```{r}
# Train models 
# (lambda changed to -0.4 because -0.89 did not produce feasible point forecasts)
arima_transformed <- train_transform |>
  model(
    bc_arima012011 = ARIMA(box_cox(Requests, -0.4) ~ pdq(0,1,2) + PDQ(0,1,1, period=12)),
    bc_arima210210 = ARIMA(box_cox(Requests, -0.4) ~ pdq(2,1,0) + PDQ(2,1,0, period = 12)),
    bc_auto = ARIMA(box_cox(Requests, -0.4)),
    log_arima100110 = ARIMA(log(Requests) ~ pdq(1,0,0) + PDQ(1,1,0)),
    log_arima004011 = ARIMA(log(Requests) ~ pdq(0,0,4) + PDQ(0,1,1)),
    log_auto = ARIMA(log(Requests)),
    arima_v = ARIMA(Requests),
    sarima_002sd = ARIMA(Requests ~ pdq(0,0,2) + PDQ(0,1,0, period=12))
  )

report(arima_transformed)

# Training Residuals 
arima_transformed |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = .innov)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.model), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Innovation Residuals by ARIMA Model",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Innovation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Validation Accuracy
val_fc2 <- arima_transformed |> 
  forecast(new_data = validation)
accuracy(val_fc2, validation) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)  |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)

# Re-examine residuals for bc-auto training fit
arima_transformed |>
  select(bc_auto) |>
  gg_tsresiduals(type = "innovation")

arima_transformed |>
  select(bc_auto) |>
  t()

```

Validation Results: Of the box-cox transformed models, the auto-selected model had the lowest AICc and RMSE. The auto log had the best metrics of all the log transformed models. Of all the arima's that were fit, the two models with the lowest RMSE were the auto-arima model with the box-cox transformation and the non-transformed seasonal ARIMA002 model. When comparing the residual plots between these two models, the box-cox transformed model remained without significant auto-correlations unlike ARIMA002. The hyperparameters that were selected for this model are: ARIMA(1,0,0)(2,1,1)\[12\] with no constants.

```{r}
# Forecast Comparisons
val_fc2 |>
  autoplot(train |> filter_index('2022 Jan' ~ .)) +
  autolayer(validation, Requests, color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.model)) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Validation Forecast vs. Actual",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Requests"
  )
```

Evaluate final ARIMA model on test set:

```{r}
# Combine training and validation sets for re-training
new_train <- bind_rows(train, validation)

# re-train final model
bc_auto <-
  new_train |>
  model(
    auto_bc = ARIMA(box_cox(Requests, -0.4))
  )
test_fc <- bc_auto |>
  forecast(new_data = test)
accuracy(test_fc, test) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 1)
test_fc |>
  autoplot(new_train) +
  autolayer(test, Requests, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Test Forecast vs. Actual",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Requests"
  )

```

Test Evaluation: Compared to the validation set, the model predicted the test set with a lower RMSE of 287.2. The 95% confidence interval is much wider than the actual test data, which may be a cause for concern. However, the point forecasts predicted the levels of the seasonal variations quite well, with the error of predicting the winter peak a few months later than the actual peak, summer troughs slightly higher than actual values and spring slightly lower than actual.
